newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl "concerned" about peace, Netanyahu flies home.
newsitem.headline: Kohl "concerned" about peace, Netanyahu flies home.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his "deep concern" at the faltering Middle East peace process on Thursday as Netanyahu cut short a visit to Bonn to face a mounting crisis at home.

Twenty-eight Palestinians were killed in clashes, taking the death toll to 33 in two days of fighting after Israel opened a controversial archaeological tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem near Islam's third-holiest shrine on Tuesday.
Israeli radio said 10 Israelis were also killed on Thursday.

"In the current situation, everything must be done, in cooperation with (Palestinian President Yasser Arafat) to prevent an escalation on both sides," a government statement quoted Kohl as telling Netanyahu in a 90-minute meeting.
"(Kohl) emphatically encouraged Netanyahu to continue his dialogue with the Palestinian side with determination on the basis of the agreements that have been concluded," the statement added.
Netanyahu flew home 5-1/2 hours earlier than planned after talking to Israeli defence officials by telephone en route to Bonn from Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in northern Germany.

Netanyahu, who came to power 100 days ago on a promise to bolster Israeli security, had been due to give a lecture in Bonn and meet German opposition leaders, parliamentary Speaker Rita Suessmuth and Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis.
He made an emergency call to Arafat during a flight from Hanover to Bonn to urge him to take "strident action" to calm tension between Palestinians and Israeli security forces.
"Arafat agreed with him and said he had already taken action in the field to calm things down," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak told reporters on the prime ministers' plane.
"Netanyahu told him it was Israel's policy not to harm holy places and therefore there was no basis for the accusations that have been made," Bazak said.
Bazak quoted Netanyahu as telling Arafat: "After things calm we should work together to advance the peace process according to agreed guidelines."
He said Israel's security cabinet would meet on Thursday evening, after Netanyahu returned to Jerusalem.
Officials in Israel said Netanyahu had also discussed a possible meeting with Arafat to try to halt the fighting.

The German government, normally at pains to stress its good relations with the Jewish state, indicated on Wednesday that its support for Israel depended on continued efforts to push ahead with the peace process.

Helmut Schaefer, state secretary in the foreign ministry, told German Radio that Bonn was worried about Netanyahu's failure to fulfil agreements signed with the Palestinians, and feared that progress towards peace might be sacrificed.

"If promises made to the extreme right in Israel are really implemented, we will have to ask if such policies can still be supported... We can't just say that, whoever rules in Israel, we'll just close our eyes and give our support," he said.
The remarks were the strongest sign yet of Bonn's concern over the way the peace process has stalled under Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's trip to Germany was the final leg of a tour of European capitals which has taken him to London and Paris.
In Bergen-Belsen, the Israeli prime minister laid wreaths to victims of the Holocaust at the memorial, and chanted the Jewish prayer for the dead.
